Short answer: no. I'd leave it alone — and not just for tactical reasons, but because it genuinely doesn't support the inference you're reaching for.

## Why the panel composition isn't a signal

The person who got the job is also a woman. Whatever happened in that room, "bias against women" cannot explain an outcome in which a woman was selected over a woman. There's no version of the sex-discrimination argument that survives that fact.

You might be reaching for something subtler — that an all-women panel had some affinity with the winning candidate that they didn't have with you. But you share the relevant characteristic with her. So the affinity theory has to rest on something other than sex, in which case the sex of the panel isn't what's doing the work.

And as a baseline matter: single-sex panels are common and unremarkable in some ministries and policy areas, in both directions. Four women on a panel is not, by itself, evidence of anything at all.

## Why raising it would cost you

You're a civil servant with ten years in. You will likely apply for other posts in this system, and the people on that panel are part of your professional environment. An unsuccessful candidate who responds to a loss by pointing at the gender of the panel — while losing to someone of the same gender — reads as someone who didn't handle the rejection well and who reaches for bad arguments under pressure. That impression is sticky and it's expensive. It will cost you far more than the complaint could ever gain you.

It also burns your credibility on the point where you actually have a legitimate grievance.

## That's the real issue

Two weeks with no response to a reasonable request for written reasons is the thing worth pursuing. Depending on your jurisdiction, you may have several overlapping entitlements:

- **A right to feedback or reasons** under the recruitment policy itself. Most civil service recruitment frameworks commit to providing feedback to shortlisted candidates, often within a specified window.
- **A subject access right** under data protection law covering personal data held about you — which in many systems includes interview notes, panel scoresheets, and assessments naming you. This usually carries a statutory deadline (often one month) and a named contact for the ministry. This is frequently the most effective route, because it's a legal obligation with a clock attached rather than a courtesy.
- **Freedom of information**, for depersonalised material like the scoring matrix, the job's essential and desirable criteria, and the weightings used.
- **An internal recruitment complaint or appeal process**, which typically has a short deadline from the date of the decision. Check that deadline now, because it may be running.

So: send a polite follow-up to whoever you originally asked, referencing your original date and request. Short, neutral, no grievance. If that produces nothing in a week or two, go to the formal routes — and be precise about which one you're invoking rather than sending another general request.

## What probably happened

Based on what you've described, the likely story is mundane. You and she probably both cleared the essential criteria comfortably. The announcement's mention of "experience of leading international projects" is doing visible work — that phrasing is typically lifted straight from a desirable criterion in the person specification. If the post involves cross-border policy work, EU or treaty files, or liaison with counterpart ministries, demonstrated leadership of international projects may have been weighted heavily, and may be the one thing you couldn't evidence as strongly.

Your law degree and your decade inside the service are real assets, but on a structured scoring matrix they only count where a criterion asks for them. A panel scoring against fixed criteria can quite easily rank a candidate with narrower credentials above a stronger generalist, if the narrow thing is what the job needs. That's not a flaw in the process; it's how the process is designed to work.

Which is exactly why you want the scoresheets. They'll tell you where you actually lost points — and that's genuinely useful for the next application in a way that a theory about the panel's composition never could be.
